newsitem.title: USA: Congress set to battle Clinton's clean air plan.
newsitem.headline: Congress set to battle Clinton's clean air plan.

text.p: Lawmakers are gearing up for an uphill battle to kill the Clinton administration's tough new limits on smog and soot in a fight that pits industrial states against those with tight pollution controls.
The new standards, endorsed by President Clinton this week, will tighten restrictions on ozone for the first time in 20 years and set the first curbs on fine particles that lodge in the lungs.

Congressmen on both sides of the aisle immediately declared war on the administration. But they face difficult odds because both parties are split on the issue, government, environmental and industry officials said Friday.

Almost 80 House Democrats and many more Republicans urged Clinton in letters to reject the Environmental Protection Agency's air quality proposal. But other Democrats and some Republicans, including Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, Republican of New York, pressed the administration to back EPA.
The American Trucking Association said Friday it will file a lawsuit challenging the EPA plan Environmental Protection Agency's plan to set tight new limits on smog and soot.
Environmentalist groups assume the White House would veto any bill to stop the EPA plan, which means opponents would have to muster two-thirds majorities in Congress to override a veto.
Anti-pollution groups said the odds in the battle were in their favour, because lawmakers would balk at voting against protecting public health.

"I'm not saying we've won and it's over," said Daniel Rosenberg, a staff attorney for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group. "But I can't imagine that they're overly confident about getting two-thirds in the House and the Senate."

In the House, the opponents of air standards are weighing several options to overturn the rules. They could block the agency from publishing the rules by a July 19 court-ordered deadline under a bill already offered, stop the rules under a new regulatory review law, withhold funds for the EPA to carry out the rules, or attempt to change the standards.

If they do not bar the official publication of the rule, lawmakers could take a stab as soon as the rules are issued, when they will have 60 working days -- essentially the rest of this congressional year -- to review the plan.
But leaders of the fight are unsure whether to use the review process as their weapon, because the law that allows Congress to overturn regulations has never been tested before.

"I think it's neither necessary nor wise to take that course," said Representative John Dingell, the top Democrat on the House Commerce Committee, who is spearheading the bid to block the new standards.

Dingell, predicting that his side would prevail, said he had talked to House and Senate Democrat and Republican leaders. "My responses as of this moment are splendid," he said in a telephone interview.

Industry groups, who say they will have to spend billions to control emissions, for little health benefit, said they were counting on cities and communities worried about losing factories and businesses to bolster their case.

"Given the number of Democratic mayors, county officials, governors, state legislators, and lawmakers saying, 'Don't do this Mr. President,' I think they've (White House officials) made a political miscalculation with their own party," said Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers Association.

"Republicans have become so gun-shy on these issues that they've ceded the moral high ground to the president," said Jonathan Adler, environmental studies director for the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank.

The trucking group that threatened a lawsuit said EPA had "failed to live up to legal provisions of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act, which requires the agency to cnosider how the standards will impact small business."
